The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty combined with the accumulating risk of macro or idiosyncratic shocks. At one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained absent a scheduled catalyst, so the interval is tighter. By one month, a wide range of outcomes becomes plausible — earnings surprises, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, or shifts in credit conditions can all compound over that window, pushing the distribution of outcomes considerably wider. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could fuel a sharp rally that overshoots the upper bound. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves in either direction, particularly around major data releases or policy meetings, and those tail events are by construction underweighted in interval estimates based on typical volatility regimes.
